strengths: Introduces a unified latent-conditioned deformable 3D Gaussian framework that jointly represents geometry, appearance, and articulation across multiple interaction states, without requiring manual part annotations.

The progressive coarse-to-fine segmentation pipeline is a reasonable engineering contribution: motion-driven separation, VLM-based part-count estimation, trajectory clustering, visibility-aware SAM prompting, and boundary-aware Gaussian splitting are integrated into one system.
Handles multi-part articulated objects with more than two interaction states and supports latent interpolation to unseen configurations, unlike several two-state/single-part baselines.
Extends the PartNet-Mobility benchmark and introduces RS-Art, a real-to-sim dataset with 18 objects, six categories, multi-state RGB-D captures, reverse-engineered meshes, and URDF/USD assets.
Reports extensive quantitative comparisons across multiple geometry and joint metrics, including objects with three movable parts, and shows generally strong improvements over baselines.
Makes a good-faith effort toward fair comparison by equalizing the per-run image budget and passing ground-truth part counts to multi-part baselines.
weaknesses: The central part-segmentation contribution is not quantitatively evaluated: there are no segmentation metrics such as IoU, part-label accuracy, or boundary accuracy, and no evaluation of VLM part-count accuracy or trajectory-clustering correctness.

Joint-type identification is technically questionable: after Kabsch alignment of the same rigid part, residuals should be near zero for both revolute and prismatic joints, so the rank-based revolute/prismatic criterion is unsupported; pivot estimation from static centroids is also unclear.

The trajectory descriptor for clustering uses raw per-Gaussian displacement directions and magnitudes. For revolute joints, points on the same rigid part have different displacement vectors depending on their distance from the joint axis, so K-means on these descriptors may not reliably group rigid parts without an explicit rigid-motion model.

Evaluation is based on single runs despite the authors acknowledging large run-to-run variance. No means, standard deviations, confidence intervals, or significance tests are reported, making the quantitative comparisons difficult to trust.

The real-world RS-Art evaluation is limited to one baseline (ArtGS), and several synthetic baselines fail or are unstable; real-world comparisons are therefore narrow, and the dataset contains only 18 objects.

Ablations are insufficient: there is no quantitative ablation of VLM part-count estimation, SAM prompt/visibility filtering, boundary-aware splitting, motion threshold, or clustering choices; the refinement ablation focuses mainly on geometry rather than segmentation quality.

Reproducibility is weak: code and data are not yet available, the VLM/SAM model versions and prompt details are underspecified, key hyperparameters such as the number of VLM queries M and τ_mot are not fully justified or sensitivity-tested.

The claim of being 'fully self-supervised' is overstated because the method relies on pretrained VLM and SAM models, which embed external semantic priors; this is not self-supervision in the usual sense.

There are clarity and notation issues: α is used for both latent code and opacity, several terms have typos ('Splitting', 'unmanual-prompt', 'interactive state'), and some metrics such as Part Motion are not clearly defined in the main text.

Methodological novelty is incremental: latent-conditioned deformation fields, SAM-based 3D segmentation, and Gaussian splitting are existing components combined into a pipeline, with limited new technical insight beyond the integration.

strengths: Unified latent-conditioned deformable Gaussian field for modeling multiple articulated states, jointly representing geometry, appearance, and motion.
Avoids manual part-count specification by inferring parts from motion trajectories, which is a practically useful direction.
Strong quantitative improvements on the expanded PartNet-Mobility split in many joint metrics (axis angle/position and part motion) versus recent baselines.
Introduces RS-Art, a real-to-sim benchmark with real RGB-D captures and reverse-engineered articulated CAD/URDF assets, addressing a real evaluation gap.
Demonstrates qualitative generalization by latent interpolation to unseen interaction states, supporting digital-twin use cases.
Code and dataset are promised for release, which would aid reproducibility.
weaknesses: The 'self-supervised' claim is weakened by dependence on a pretrained VLM to estimate the number of moved components and on SAM for segmentation; these external models are supervised and the VLM count can be brittle.

The VLM-based part count estimation is a critical single point of failure and is evaluated only by mode over M queries; no error analysis, prompt sensitivity, or fallback for wrong predictions is provided.

Technical novelty is incremental: it combines dynamic 3D Gaussian deformation with trajectory K-means and SAM-based refinement; the core ideas are largely existing components adapted to articulated objects.

Evaluation protocol is not rigorous: baselines are reported as 'first run' due to variance rather than mean/std over multiple seeds/runs, making claimed stability difficult to verify and potentially cherry-picked.
The abstract/claim 'outperforms existing methods' is overstated: Ours is not best on all metrics (e.g., CD-s and CD-w on some categories), and RS-Art compares only ArtGS, not all baselines.
Important implementation details are missing or unclear in the main paper: τ_mot value, M, exact VLM/SAM versions, state sampling, and K-means robustness criteria are not fully specified.
Notation is confusing: α is used for Gaussian opacity and latent code, and z_k vs α_k are inconsistent; this hurts clarity and reproducibility.
The boundary-aware splitting follows SAGD closely and relies on external SAM masks; the 'unsupervised' segmentation is therefore not fully self-contained.
RS-Art is relatively small (18 objects in 6 categories) and its ground truth is manually reverse-engineered, which limits generalization claims and may introduce author-dependent bias.
Ablations are incomplete: no comparison against alternative clustering, no VLM count ablation, no sensitivity to camera pose noise despite the real-data claim.
Failure cases and limitations are acknowledged only briefly; the method still needs accurate camera poses and cannot handle fully occluded regions, which are significant practical constraints.

strengths: Proposes a unified deformable 3D Gaussian representation with latent-conditioned deformation across multiple interaction states, enabling continuous articulation modeling and independent part control without manual part annotations.

Introduces a well-motivated progressive coarse-to-fine segmentation pipeline: motion-driven separation, VLM-based part-count estimation, trajectory clustering, visibility-guided SAM prompting, and boundary-aware Gaussian splitting.

Reports strong quantitative improvements on an expanded PartNet-Mobility benchmark, especially for joint parameter and part-motion metrics, and qualitative generalization to unseen interaction states.
Contributes a new real-to-sim benchmark (RS-Art) with real RGB-D captures and reverse-engineered articulated digital twins, which is valuable for the community.
Ablation studies support key design choices, including the benefit of the refinement stage and the importance of using more than two interaction states.
The paper is clearly written and the overall pipeline is logically structured and reproducible in principle, with code and datasets promised.
weaknesses: Evaluation reports only a single run per method and lacks error bars or statistical significance tests, despite acknowledging large run-to-run variance in baselines; this weakens the reliability of the reported superiority.
The VLM-based part-count estimation is a critical component but is not quantitatively evaluated; no analysis is provided for prompt sensitivity, failure modes, or the downstream impact of miscounts.

Several heuristics and thresholds (e.g., motion threshold, visibility threshold, recursive splitting stopping criteria, K-means initialization) lack sensitivity analysis, and runtime/ computational cost is not reported.

Baseline comparison has fairness concerns: ArticulatedGS is reproduced without official code, single-part baselines are run per joint with more total images, and baseline failures marked with asterisks are not analyzed in detail.
The RS-Art dataset is a useful contribution, but the main-paper quantitative evaluation is limited to only one baseline (ArtGS) and the dataset contains 18 objects, which limits statistical strength.

The claim of being 'fully self-supervised' should be tempered: the method still relies on an external VLM and various hand-tuned thresholds, and no manual annotations are not the same as being free of priors or heuristics.

Joint type identification and parameter estimation are not evaluated under challenging cases such as screw joints, near-static motion, or heavily coupled articulation, which are acknowledged as limitations but remain unaddressed.

strengths: Introduces a unified latent-conditioned deformable Gaussian splatting framework for articulated objects that can model an arbitrary number of interaction states as continuous deformations of a shared canonical field, going beyond the restrictive two-state, single-joint assumptions of prior work.

Proposes a coarse-to-fine part segmentation pipeline that combines motion-trajectory clustering, VLM-based part-count estimation, visibility-aware SAM prompting, and boundary-aware Gaussian splitting; the design is reasonably novel and well motivated by the need for part-level decoupling without manual part labels.

Releases the RS-Art dataset, which pairs real multi-view RGB-D captures of articulated objects with reverse-engineered part-level 3D models and URDF annotations. This is a useful contribution for real-to-sim evaluation and for benchmarking sim-to-real generalization.

Provides extensive experiments across multiple categories, multiple instances, and objects with 2, 3, and 5 movable parts. The method consistently performs strongly on joint parameter estimation and part-level geometry metrics, often by large margins over competitive baselines.

Includes informative ablations on the refinement stage, number of interaction states, VLM prompting strategies, SAM-based segmentation, camera pose robustness, and runtime, which help validate the design choices and support reproducibility.
weaknesses: Several technical details are underspecified, which hurts reproducibility and makes some central claims harder to verify. In particular, the density similarity term L_D_SIMM in Eq. 7 is not defined, and the architecture/dimension of the deformation MLP, latent code size, and optimization hyperparameters are not given in the main paper or appendix excerpt.

The motion descriptor used for coarse part clustering is defined using ordered transitions between consecutive states (Eq. 9), but it is not explained how an arbitrary set of discrete interaction states is ordered. If the states are unordered, the descriptor and resulting clustering can change arbitrarily, which is a methodological gap.

For revolute parts, per-Gaussian displacement directions and magnitudes can vary significantly across a single rigid part depending on distance to the joint axis. The coarse K-means grouping based on such motion descriptors may therefore not reliably group whole rigid parts; the method relies on later SAM/boundary refinement to correct this, but the justification and robustness of the coarse stage are not sufficiently analyzed.

The main comparison is not fully apples-to-apples. The proposed method uses four interaction states, while the dominant two-state baselines use only two states and in some cases receive known part counts and additional depth. Although an appendix experiment with two states is provided, the main tables may overstate the benefit from having more states than the baselines are designed to use.

The evaluation reports the first run for each baseline due to high variance rather than mean and standard deviation over multiple runs. This weakens the statistical strength of the comparisons, even though the authors state the numbers are not cherry-picked.

The claim of collision-free interpolation in continuous deformation is not quantitatively verified. The paper shows qualitative interpolation results, but no collision metric, physical plausibility check, or downstream task evaluation is provided to substantiate the claim of reliable continuous control.

Some important implementation details, such as whether and how the VLM component may fail on certain categories, the exact K-means initialization/merging procedure, and the effect of the static/dynamic threshold, are not explored in sufficient depth. The dataset RS-Art is valuable but relatively small (18 objects), and its reverse-engineered ground truth still involves manual modeling effort.

strengths: Addresses an important and challenging problem: self-supervised part-level modeling and continuous control of articulated objects from multi-view images.
Introduces a latent-conditioned deformation of a canonical 3D Gaussian field, enabling interpolation to unseen interaction states and part-aware reconstruction.
Contributes an expanded PartNet-Mobility evaluation split and the RS-Art real-to-sim dataset, which could be useful for future benchmarking.
Integrates VLM/SAM components for part counting and boundary refinement, and includes a range of experiments on synthetic and real data.
Reports promising quantitative and qualitative results on several multi-part and multi-state settings, including ablations on refinement and number of interaction states.
weaknesses: The core deformation field lacks explicit part-level rigidity or coherence constraints during optimization. Each Gaussian is transformed independently via a shared latent-conditioned MLP, and parts are only discovered post-hoc by clustering motion trajectories. There is no mechanism enforcing that primitives belonging to the same rigid part follow a common transformation, so the central claim of unsupervised part-level decoupling is not technically guaranteed.

The joint type identification and parameter estimation appear mathematically flawed. Kabsch alignment of corresponding points under both revolute and prismatic motion should yield near-zero residuals because both are rigid transformations; the proposed singular-value rank criterion cannot reliably distinguish them. For revolute joints, the pivot is fitted using static centroids, which is incorrect for finding the axis of a moving part. These issues undermine the claimed accurate kinematic modeling.

The evaluation is not sufficiently rigorous for a top-tier venue. Baselines are run only once without mean/std or statistical significance, despite the paper acknowledging large run-to-run variance. Some baselines fail or are marked with stars, and there is no systematic analysis of failures. The comparison also mixes different input budgets: single-part baselines are run per part and consume 200 × n_parts images, while the proposed method uses 200 images total, and two-state baselines use a different state/input regime. Real-data evaluation only compares against ArtGS because other baselines allegedly fail, which weakens the sim-to-real evidence.

Some reported metrics do not support the broad claim of outperforming prior methods. For example, on the synthetic PartNet-Mobility mean, DTArt achieves a lower CD-w than the proposed method (2.18 vs. 3.02), and several per-category geometry metrics are worse than baselines. The paper does not adequately discuss or explain these cases.

Important technical details are missing or unclear. The loss term L_D_SIMM is introduced but never defined formally. The symbol α is used both for Gaussian opacity and for the latent state code, causing notational confusion. Several sections contain typos and inconsistencies, e.g., '3D Gaussian Splitting' instead of Splatting, and joint parameter equations that do not match the written explanation.

The novelty is incremental: the method largely combines existing ideas from dynamic 3D Gaussian splatting, latent-conditioned deformation, K-means trajectory clustering, VLM prompting, and SAM/SAGD-based boundary splitting. The part-decoupling is mostly a post-processing pipeline rather than a jointly learned structured representation.

The VLM-based component-count estimation is brittle and only validated on a small set of instances. The reported 100% accuracy is suspiciously high and lacks robustness analysis across prompts, object categories, and VLM choices; the ablation already shows a generic cross-state prompt achieves only 15% accuracy.

Reproducibility is limited: code and dataset are promised only upon publication, several implementation details are deferred to an appendix that may not be fully self-contained, and the training/inference comparisons in Table 10 raise questions about whether the baselines were tuned fairly.

strengths: Introduces a unified latent-conditioned deformable 3DGS framework for articulated objects that jointly models geometry, appearance, and kinematics across arbitrary interaction states, addressing limitations of prior two-state/single-part methods.

Coarse-to-fine part segmentation is well motivated and technically sound: motion-trajectory clustering, VLM-based part count estimation, visibility-aware SAM prompting, and boundary-aware Gaussian splitting together enable automatic part decoupling without manual part labels.

Strong empirical results on expanded PartNet-Mobility, including multi-part and three/five-part objects, with clear improvements over PARIS, ArticulatedGS, DTArt, and ArtGS on most kinematic and geometry metrics.
The release of RS-Art, a real-to-sim RGB-D benchmark with reverse-engineered URDF/USD models and multi-state captures, is a valuable community contribution and enables more realistic evaluation.
Demonstrates continuous deformation and generalization to unseen interaction states via latent interpolation, with quantitative and qualitative comparisons against dynamic NeRF/3DGS baselines.

Ablations validate key components, including the refinement stage, number of interaction states, VLM prompting strategy, and SAM segmentation, and the appendix provides substantial implementation detail.
weaknesses: Some notational and presentation issues reduce clarity, e.g., α is used both for latent state codes and per-Gaussian opacity, n_part vs. n_parts is inconsistent, and the density-similarity loss L_{DSIMM} is not formally defined.

The deformation network is trained mainly with photometric and density-similarity objectives, without an explicit part-rigidity or trajectory-coherence regularizer during optimization; part semantics rely on post-hoc clustering and may be fragile when motion is small or states are sparse, as also suggested by the K=2 ablation.

The main comparisons give PD2GS four interaction states while several baselines are two-state methods, so the benefit of additional state observations is partly confounded with method quality; the two-state result in the appendix helps but is not the headline comparison.
Evaluation reports only the first run for several baselines, with no mean/std or statistical significance, making the reported gains harder to assess despite the stated run-to-run variance.

Some claims, such as collision-free trajectories and robust real-world generalization, are supported mainly qualitatively or on a limited set of real objects; broader real-data comparisons are constrained by baseline failures.
The method depends on pretrained VLM and SAM modules and accurate camera poses; robustness to pose noise and VLM/SAM errors is only partially evaluated.
